title: Variarum Libri Duodecim
author: Cassiodorus

passages.original: 0 quaM arduum est subjectum verba dominantis assumere, loqui posse quod nostrum credatur, et provecti in publicum decorem gloriosam facere felicitatem! Considerate quid ponderis habeatis pariter et decoris. c Si quid dubitamus, a quæstore requirimus, qui est a thesaurus famæ publicæ, armarium legum, paratus semper ad subitum; et, ut ait Tullius, magister eloquentiæ, nihil praestabilius videtur quam posse dicen- do tenere hominum metentes, allicere voluntates, im- pellere quo velit, unde aUlcm-velit dedocere. Nam si oratoris est proprium graviter et ornate dicere, ut possit animos judicum commovere, quanto facundior debet esse qui ore principis populos noscitur admonere, ut recta diligant, perversa contemnant, bonos sine fine laudent, pessimos vehementer accusent ?
passages.english: O how arduous it is for a subject to take up the words of the ruler, to be able to speak what may be believed to be ours, and, advanced to public honour, to make [our] felicity glorious! Consider how much weight you hold, and equally how much honour. If we are in doubt about anything, we ask the quaestor, who is the treasury of public reputation, the cabinet of the laws, always ready for the sudden need; and, as Tullius, the master of eloquence, says, nothing seems more excellent than to be able by speaking to hold the minds of men, to attract their wills, to drive them where one wishes, and to lead them away from where one wishes. For if it is the proper task of the orator to speak with gravity and ornament, so that he can move the minds of judges, how much more eloquent ought he to be who is known to admonish peoples with the mouth of the prince, so that they may love what is right, despise what is perverse, praise the good without end, and vehemently accuse the worst?
passages.notes: Opening '0 quaM' read as 'O quam'; stray 'c' and 'a' taken as footnote marks. 'metentes' read as 'mentes'; 'aUlcm-velit' read as 'unde autem velit' or similar, rendered 'from where one wishes'. Tullius is Cicero (De oratore 1.30).
